text: With 10% down at the September 2026 average 30-year rate (6.862%), the original schedule brings the loan to 80% of the purchase price after 99 payments and to 78% after 114: about 8 to 9.5 years of mortgage insurance if home values are ignored.

Measured against the national home-price index instead, buyers who put 10% down in 307 purchase months from January 1991 to July 2016 reached a loan of 80% of the index value after a median of 23 months; 14.7% needed more than 60 months, and October 2005 buyers needed 112.
note: Same set B for every number; 112 is the T of the 2005-10 purchase month itself.

text: At the two-year mark, 58.6% of 403 purchase months (1991-2024) were at or below 80% of index value, but only 15.6% were at or below 75%.
note: Both shares over the same set A at k=24.
Check: every month used is an observed month (lastA + 24 = hpi_last); nothing extrapolated.

text: Buyers expect to pay mortgage insurance for most of a decade, until the loan is paid down to 80% of what they paid; price gains are rarely counted.
note: Guess about beliefs; the check is that the schedule-only figure is 'most of a decade' (60 < sched80 <= 120). Not evidence of what buyers believe.

text: The years of insurance a 10%-down buyer is pricing in are usually the schedule's 8+ years;
note: Check: sched80 >= 96 months. Part 2 of the sentence is statement 7.

text: national price history says equity on paper often reached 80% in about two years, but not reliably (one in seven purchase months took over five years, and lender value-based rules are stricter).
The viewer can compare the real range, not one number, with the extra years of renting needed to reach 20%.
note: Check: the range is non-degenerate (min < median < max, set B: 13 < 23 < 112). Renting years are not modeled.

text: A national index hides large local and individual differences.
note: Qualitative; national data cannot measure local spread. Check only that even the national index has slow cases (max > 60).

text: Removal based on current value is set by the lender or investor (appraisal, minimum seasoning, often 75% in early years), so the index result is an upper bound on how early removal was possible.
note: Check: for every set-B month, the first month at <= 75% is never earlier than at <= 80%.

text: The law-based schedule (80% request, 78% automatic) depends only on the original value.
note: Check: sched80 < sched78 (computed without the index).

text: The 23-month median is when the loan reached 80% of a national index value.
at the two-year mark only 15.6% of purchase months were at or below 75%.
October 2005 buyers took 112 months, and 14.7% of purchase months took over five years.

By law the borrower may request cancellation when the scheduled balance reaches 80% of original value and it ends automatically at 78% (with conditions such as being current on payments); value-based removal is a lender or investor rule, not the law.
note: Legal text in sources.json provisions; numeric check: sched80 < sched78.

text: Sets A and B use only purchase months with enough later data (24 or more than 120 months), so recent buyers are only in set A.
Using decades of home prices and mortgage rates, we measure how long mortgage insurance actually had to stay for buyers who put 10% down.
note: Check: index span >= 20 years (1991-2026). RISK: 'actually had to stay' overstates; the index result is equity on paper, not removal (result.assumptions[3]). Suggest 'how long it took, on paper, to reach 80%'.
